analysis.one_liner: Lets federally insured banks keep trading riskier derivatives by loosening Dodd-Frank's swaps firewall.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill never advanced past its committee referral and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 crisis, Dodd-Frank banned banks with federal deposit insurance and access to Federal Reserve and FDIC backstops from trading certain swaps — derivatives tied to bundles of loans — and required that business to be moved to affiliates without those taxpayer protections. This bill would have reversed much of that: it would let insured banks keep trading swaps backed by asset-backed securities, extend the carve-outs to U.S. branches of foreign banks, and repeal limits on which derivatives banks could keep [S2] [S3]. In plain terms, it reopens the door for banks to do riskier derivatives trading inside the part of the bank that taxpayers stand behind.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and derivatives dealers, including foreign banks' U.S. branches, gain by keeping lucrative swaps trading inside federally backstopped entities instead of moving it to separately capitalized affiliates [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would replace Dodd-Frank's narrow exemption with broader permission for 'covered depository institutions' — FDIC-insured banks and uninsured U.S. branches of foreign banks — to keep swaps business in-house, limited to hedging, non-structured swaps, and certain structured finance swaps [S2] [S3].

It would let banks keep trading structured finance swaps (derivatives based on asset-backed securities) for hedging or where regulators authorize the underlying securities — reversing the push-out of the riskiest derivatives [S2] [S3].

It would repeal the existing narrow exemption conditions for credit default swaps and rate swaps, and drop the requirement that a bank's affiliate not be an insured institution in order to do this business [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the FDIC insurance fund bear the risk: the ban exists so that losses on speculative derivatives are not covered by federal backstops meant for depositors. Weakening it means derivatives losses inside an insured bank could again land on the safety net [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the original provision pushed ordinary hedging activity out of insured banks and toward less-regulated foreign entities, raising costs for banks and their customers; the bill kept the requirement that in-house swaps be hedging or risk-mitigating in most cases [S2] [S3].

The core cost an honest supporter must acknowledge: the bill widens the range of asset-backed derivatives that insured banks can hold, partially undoing a firewall Congress built so that federal deposit insurance and Fed credit do not subsidize speculative derivatives trading [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to a concentrated set of large banks that would save the cost of ring-fencing derivatives operations; the cost is diffuse — more taxpayer exposure if derivatives losses hit an insured bank. The bill keeps some hedging limits, but its main effect is expanding what backstopped banks can trade, so the balance favors the industry over the public's interest in a clean firewall.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kay Hagan introduced the bill on March 6, 2013, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Toomey, Warner, and Johanns [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No further action — no committee vote and no floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, Dodd-Frank's prohibition on federal assistance to swaps entities stayed intact for the time being, and the banks that would have gained from moving risky derivatives back inside insured entities did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the Dodd-Frank swaps firewall held

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; it never came to a committee vote or the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic lead sponsor with two Republicans and one more Democrat among the three cosponsors — but the bill never progressed far enough for a recorded party split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have let FDIC-insured banks keep asset-backed and other derivatives trading in-house rather than pushing it to uninsured affiliates, preserving lucrative dealing revenue behind the federal safety net. Its gain came at the cost of greater taxpayer backstop exposure.

industries.industry: U.S. branches and agencies of foreign banks
industries.note: The bill explicitly extends the exemption from the federal-assistance prohibition to uninsured U.S. branches of foreign banks, letting them access covered-bank treatment for swaps activities.
By authorizing structured finance swaps based on asset-backed securities inside insured banks, the bill would have restored a buyer base for securitized products that Dodd-Frank pushed out.
